sections.model_projection: The model projects Green Bay 23.19, Minnesota 22.94, for a near pick-em game with a projected total of 46.13. Green Bay's win probability sits at 45.9% despite being the away team, while the market has Minnesota as a 1.5-point home favorite. The model's margin lands 1.75 points more favorable to Green Bay than the market spread, though the total is within half a point of the market's 46.5. All metrics carry a low-sample flag as this is Week 1 with no 2026 games played.
sections.offensive_matchup: Green Bay's offense enters as one of the most efficient in the league, ranking 2nd in EPA per play (a measure of how many expected points each play adds) at +0.164, while Minnesota's offense ranks 27th at -0.110. The Packers convert 48.9% of plays successfully (4th) compared to the Vikings' 42.4% (22nd), meaning Green Bay consistently moves the chains while Minnesota struggles to generate positive plays. Minnesota's defense is legitimately elite, however, ranking 4th in defensive EPA per play at -0.078 and holding opponents to a 41.3% success rate (4th), so the Vikings' defense will push back hard against Green Bay's efficient attack. The Vikings' offense faces a Green Bay defense that ranks a middling 21st in defensive EPA per play, which gives Minnesota's struggling unit a path to points if it can get out of its own way.
sections.quarterback_edge: Jordan Love holds a clear career edge over Kyler Murray in this matchup. Love has posted a career EPA per dropback of +0.159 across 53 games and 1,665 attempts, with a 7.54 yards per attempt average and a 63.8% completion rate. Murray, flagged as a new-team starter in Minnesota, carries a career EPA per dropback of just +0.027 across 55 games and 1,882 attempts, with a 6.86 yards per attempt average. The quarterback edge is the single largest factor in the model, contributing 0.71 points toward Green Bay, reflecting a meaningful gap in career efficiency between the two signal-callers.
sections.trenches: Minnesota's defensive front is the strongest trench advantage in this game, ranking 3rd in sack rate (9.3% of dropbacks) and 2nd in pressure rate (29.3%), and it generates that pressure even without blitzing — ranking 2nd in pressure without blitz at 18.1%. Green Bay's offensive line ranks 8th in sack rate allowed (5.0%) and 1st in havoc allowed (meaning opponents generate the fewest disruptive plays against them), so the Packers' protection is legitimately good, but Minnesota's front is elite enough that this is still a meaningful edge for the Vikings worth 0.32 points in the model. On the flip side, Minnesota's offensive line is one of the most vulnerable in the league, ranking 31st in sack rate allowed (10.4%) and 30th in havoc allowed (17.9%), while Green Bay's pass rush ranks 7th in pressure rate (27.0%) and 8th in pressure without blitz (14.4%). Green Bay's defensive front should be able to create problems for Murray behind a porous Vikings line.
sections.explosive_play_edge: Green Bay generates explosive plays — defined as rushes of 10-plus yards or passes of 20-plus yards — on 11.1% of plays, ranking 3rd in the league, while Minnesota produces them on just 8.1% of plays (21st). Minnesota's defense limits explosive plays reasonably well at 7.5% allowed (6th), but Green Bay's defense allows them at a slightly higher 7.9% rate (10th), giving the Packers a net edge in the big-play dimension worth 0.26 points. This gap matters because explosive plays are disproportionately responsible for scoring drives, and Green Bay's ability to create them against a Vikings defense that is otherwise stout could be the difference in a close game.
sections.third_down_red_zone: The third-down disparity in this game is stark: Green Bay converts 48.0% of third downs (3rd in the league), while Minnesota converts just 32.3% (dead last, 32nd). Minnesota's defense does hold opponents to a 34.5% third-down rate (2nd best), so the Packers will face resistance, but Green Bay's own defense allows a 41.5% conversion rate (20th), giving Murray's offense a reasonable chance to extend drives. In the red zone, Green Bay scores touchdowns on 69.2% of trips (4th) and averages 3.30 points per scoring opportunity (6th), while Minnesota scores touchdowns on just 54.0% of red-zone trips (24th) and averages 2.82 points per opportunity (20th). Minnesota's red-zone defense is strong at 51.0% touchdowns allowed (5th), but Green Bay's finishing efficiency still represents a meaningful edge.
sections.roster_talent: Green Bay carries a roster continuity index of 0.87, meaning a high share of its production returns from prior seasons, with 90% of passing production and 69% of rushing production back. Minnesota's continuity index is lower at 0.78, though its returning production numbers are strong in some areas — 100% of passing production returns and 83% of receiving production, though the new-team-starter flag on Murray complicates the passing continuity figure. Green Bay's offensive line returns 57 combined starts of experience, while Minnesota's line returns 69, giving the Vikings a slight edge in experienced blockers despite their poor protection metrics. Talent ratings are unavailable for both teams per the data package.
sections.recent_form: Insufficient reliable data. This is Week 1 of the 2026 season and neither team has played a game, so no recent form data exists. The model assigns a neutral form shift of 0.0 for both teams.
sections.market_movement: The market opened Green Bay at Minnesota -1.5 on the spread with a total of 46.5, and as of the most recent snapshot across 162 observations from nine books, both lines have held completely steady with zero movement on the spread and zero movement on the total. The moneyline sits at Minnesota -122 / Green Bay +102, implying a no-vig home win probability of 52.6%. There is a 0.5-point book disagreement on the spread across the nine books sampled. Public betting percentages are unavailable, so no claim about ticket or money distribution can be made.
key_advantages: Green Bay holds a significant quarterback efficiency edge: Jordan Love's career EPA per dropback (+0.159) is nearly six times Kyler Murray's (+0.027)
Packers rank 3rd in explosive play rate (11.1%) and 3rd in third-down conversion (48.0%), giving them multiple ways to sustain and finish drives
Green Bay's offensive havoc allowed ranks 1st, meaning opponents generate the fewest disruptive plays against their offense, helping Love operate cleanly
Minnesota's defense is elite (4th in EPA per play allowed, 2nd in third-down rate allowed), providing a genuine floor for the Vikings even when their offense struggles
key_concerns: Minnesota's defensive front ranks 3rd in sack rate and 2nd in pressure rate, threatening to disrupt Love behind a Packers line that still allowed pressure on 20.4% of dropbacks

Green Bay's defense ranks only 21st in EPA per play allowed and 20th in third-down rate allowed, leaving the door open for Murray and a Vikings offense that uses play-action on 27.7% of dropbacks (9th)

Minnesota's turnover margin of -0.41 per game (27th) is a structural concern, but Green Bay's defense ranks 30th in havoc rate, limiting its ability to force the turnovers that would capitalize on Viking mistakes
All metrics carry a low-sample flag with zero 2026 games played, and Kyler Murray's new-team-starter flag introduces uncertainty about how quickly he adapts to Minnesota's system
sections.expected_game_script: Green Bay figures to control the offensive tempo early, leaning on Jordan Love's passing efficiency against a Vikings secondary that ranked 24th in passing EPA allowed. Minnesota's defensive front will apply consistent pressure — even without blitzing, they rank 2nd in generating pressure — so Love will need to process quickly and get the ball out, which aligns with the Packers' 1st-ranked havoc-allowed mark suggesting their protection scheme handles disruption well. On the other side, Kyler Murray will face a Green Bay pass rush that generates pressure on 27.0% of dropbacks behind a Vikings offensive line that allowed sacks on 10.4% of dropbacks (31st), meaning Murray could spend much of the game under duress in his first start with Minnesota. Minnesota's offense is most likely to find success through play-action (27.7% rate, 9th) and the run game, where both teams are roughly even in rushing EPA, rather than through traditional dropbacks where the Vikings rank 29th in passing EPA per play. The Vikings' elite defense — particularly their ability to hold opponents to a 34.5% third-down rate — keeps them competitive even if their offense sputters, and home field adds a meaningful 1.5 points to their ledger. The most likely outcome is a close, low-scoring game where Green Bay's finishing efficiency in the red zone (69.2% touchdown rate) and third-down conversion advantage (48.0% vs. 32.3%) prove to be the deciding factors in a game the model projects as essentially a coin flip at 23-23.
